claims.text: High configurational entropy kinetically stabilizes the disordered structure of near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles at elevated temperatures.
High configurational entropy results in lattice distortion in near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles.
Suppression of elemental diffusion inhibits phase segregation.
The initial nanoparticles have a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial nanoparticles possess inherent lattice strain.
A slight deviation from an equiatomic composition reduces configurational entropy relative to the near-equiatomic control.
Uniform atomic-scale mixing is associated with local compressive and tensile lattice strains.
Local compressive and tensile lattice strains inhibit atomic diffusion.
High configurational entropy lowers the free energy of the disordered phase.
Lattice distortions create kinetic barriers to elemental diffusion and phase separation.
Reducing configurational entropy through a slight compositional deviation lowers diffusion or phase-separation barriers.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles will preserve a single-phase solid-solution structure better than off-equiatomic nanoparticles during identical high-temperature exposure.
Off-equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit phase segregation or ordering earlier than near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
The proposed stabilization effect is significant only in a nanoparticle size regime where surface effects do not dominate.
Minimizing oxidation and external chemical reactions is necessary to isolate thermal stability under the proposed conditions.
